A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VISE benchmark and mitigation methods. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and relocation.

before.justification: v2 reports original Video-LLM evaluations, mitigation experiments, attention analyses, ablations and qualitative cases in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds mitigation comparisons, neutral-question accuracy tests, relaxed-response experiments and Gemini-2.5-Flash evaluations.

M1.justification: Both versions retain neutral-prompt key-frame selection and inference-time representation steering, including the appendix PCA-subspace intervention. v3 condenses explanations and adds an illustration without establishing a changed algorithm, calibration procedure or intervention.

E1.justification: The MSVD, MSRVTT and NExT-QA coverage, 367 videos, 6,367 questions and seven sycophancy scenarios are retained. Added experiments reuse this video-QA coverage; relaxed response formatting changes the protocol rather than the underlying task.

E2.justification: v3 Section 5.3/Table 4 adds majority voting and contradiction-checking prompting as evaluated alternatives to both mitigation methods on Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Appendix G also adds Gemini-2.5-Flash to the commercial-model comparison. Existing comparators remain.

E3.justification: v3 adds neutral-question accuracy evaluation over 6,367 questions and a relaxed-response protocol with manual classification of misleading and non-committal answers across five scenarios. The new majority-vote comparator uses three sampled decoding paths. These expand evaluation procedures without replacing the original benchmark protocol.

E4.justification: New Appendices A and D test whether mitigation harms ordinary answering accuracy and whether restricting responses to option letters drives observed sycophancy. These address important validation questions absent from v2. Existing frame-count, random-selection, architecture-failure, attention and steering-strength analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seed-based replication, confidence intervals or formal significance tests. The CRS small-sample warning and attention displays are retained. Three sampled paths in the new voting baseline define that comparator, not an uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Existing numerical tables retain their values after matching relocations and transpositions. New results include average MSS of 44.71 for majority voting and 52.84 for contradiction prompting, neutral-accuracy losses of 1.13–3.74 percentage points, and relaxed-response misleading/non-committal rates of 36.00%/4.45%. Gemini-2.5-Flash adds average MSS/CRS of 64.39/20.09.

T1.justification: The MSS/CRS notation is simplified to correct-to-incorrect and incorrect-to-correct counts without changing the definitions. Attention metrics, separability calculations and PCA intervention derivations are retained, with the steering appendix moving from F to H. No new proof or formal theoretical result appears.

C1.justification: The introduction narrows its research-gap claim: v3 acknowledges temporally rich video diagnostics and complex reasoning benchmarks, emphasizing their lack of targeted user-feedback sycophancy evaluation. The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the benchmark and two mitigation contributions.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations concerning systematic versus decoding-noise errors, response-format dependence, preservation of ordinary accuracy and regression in newer commercial models. It also introduces an orthogonality interpretation for steering and explicit limitations concerning white-box access, hour-scale videos and agentic tasks. These substantially extend the scientific discussion.

D1.justification: The abstract changes the supplied code-access location from GitHub to an anonymous.4open.science repository. v3 documents three-path voting and manual response classification for new experiments. Existing hardware, separate 100-video calibration set, selected layers and PCA settings remain documented.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands citations concerning sycophancy, activation steering, multimodal trustworthiness and retrieval-based reasoning. The introduction and Related Work revise positioning to distinguish sycophancy from existing temporal-reasoning and factuality diagnostics. Missing steering citations are also resolved; bibliographic updates alone are excluded from this judgment.

P1.justification: Rewriting is concentrated in the introduction, Related Work and condensed key-frame explanation. v3 relocates limitations and calibration qualifications, removes the LLM-use declaration, and adds ethics and acknowledgements text. Most existing narrative and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 changes the document from one-column to two-column layout, transposes both main mitigation tables and relocates the complex-question table to Appendix B. It adds five result tables and a key-frame illustration. Existing benchmark, attention and case figures are retained, with resizing and relocation.

improvement.justification: v2 lacked standard mitigation alternatives and quantified neutral-accuracy costs; v3 addresses these gaps in Tables 4 and 5. Table 8 additionally tests response-format dependence, substantially strengthening the empirical validation of both mitigation and benchmark design. The new checks cover limited model families, and accuracy preservation does not establish the claimed representation orthogonality, but the added controls provide a substantial net improvement.
